sentences.text: Asteracanthus was one of the largest known hybodonts, reaching lengths of 2 to 3 meters.
Its teeth were high-crowned and multi-cusped, designed for specific feeding tasks.
Unlike other hybodonts, the fin spines of this animal were covered in tubercles rather than ribbing.
A complete skeleton of this creature was described in 2021 from the Late Jurassic Solnhofen Limestone.
Evidence suggests Asteracanthus may have scavenged on marine reptiles.
This predator was adapted for open marine environments and likely swam just above the seafloor.
Researchers suggest Asteracanthus used its teeth for grasping prey, with side teeth adapted for crushing.
It likely fed on a diverse diet including fish, crustaceans, echinoderms, molluscs, and cephalopods like belemnites.
Asteracanthus is classified as a member of the class Chondrichthyes, order Hybodontiformes, and family Hybodontidae.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Asteracanthus as Acrodontinae and the family as Acrodontidae.
The genus Asteracanthus is now considered distinct from Strophodus, with its teeth being more similar to those of Hybodus and Egertonodus.
Fossils of Asteracanthus have been found in Europe, including Germany, Switzerland, England, and France.
